# GarkpitMediator (@garkpit/mediator): the complete manual

> A small, zero-dependency CQRS mediator for TypeScript web apps. Every feature is a named Command or Query with exactly one handler, sent through one pipeline of shared behaviors (locking, auditing, logging, or your own). The result is a codebase that people and AI coding agents can both find their way around as it grows, and an app whose capabilities can be handed to a chat assistant or an MCP server as tools.

Source: https://github.com/garkpit/GarkpitMediator (MIT). This file is every guide joined together, generated from docs/*.md.

---

<!-- docs/getting-started.md -->

# Getting started

`@garkpit/mediator` is a small TypeScript library that gives every feature in your app one front door.
Each thing the app can do is a named class: a **Command** if it changes something, a **Query** if it
only reads. You hand one to the **mediator** (the object that knows which piece of code handles which
request) and it runs the one handler registered for that class, wrapped in whatever shared steps you
have installed: locking, an audit record, a log line, or your own.

It has no runtime dependencies and ships as TypeScript source. It runs on [Bun](https://bun.sh) and on
any bundler that compiles TypeScript.

## Install: copy it in

There is no npm package. You copy the source into your project and record which commit you took. The
copy is called a *synced export*: a folder you never edit by hand and replace wholesale when you want
a newer version.

```sh
# 1. Fetch the library somewhere outside your app
git clone https://github.com/garkpit/GarkpitMediator.git ../GarkpitMediator

# 2. Copy the library files (not the docs site or examples) into your app
mkdir -p packages/mediator
git -C ../GarkpitMediator archive HEAD src package.json tsconfig.json LICENSE README.md llms-full.txt \
  | tar -x -C packages/mediator

# 3. Record where it came from
echo "Source: https://github.com/garkpit/GarkpitMediator at $(git -C ../GarkpitMediator rev-parse HEAD)" \
  > packages/mediator/SOURCE.md
```

Then make it a workspace package. In your app's `package.json`:

```json
{
  "workspaces": ["packages/*"],
  "dependencies": {
    "@garkpit/mediator": "workspace:*"
  }
}
```

Run `bun install` and import from `@garkpit/mediator`. The copied folder includes `llms-full.txt`, the
whole manual as one text file, so a coding agent working in your repository can read how the library
works without leaving it. See [Working with AI coding agents](ai-coding-agents.md).

Prefer no workspace? Copy just `src/` to somewhere like `src/lib/mediator/` and import it by relative
path. Everything on this site works the same way.

## Your first Command and Query

```ts
import { Command, Query, createMediator, LoggingBehavior } from '@garkpit/mediator';

interface Note {
  id: string;
  title: string;
}
const notes = new Map<string, Note>();

// A Query reads. Its type parameter is what the handler returns.
class GetNote extends Query<Note | undefined> {
  constructor(readonly id: string) {
    super();
  }
}

// A Command changes something.
class AddNote extends Command<Note> {
  constructor(readonly title: string) {
    super();
  }
}

// One mediator for the app. LoggingBehavior prints one line per request.
const mediator = createMediator({ behaviors: [new LoggingBehavior()] });

// Exactly one handler per request class.
mediator.register(GetNote, { handle: async (query) => notes.get(query.id) });
mediator.register(AddNote, {
  handle: async (command) => {
    const note = { id: `n${notes.size + 1}`, title: command.title };
    notes.set(note.id, note);
    return note;
  }
});

// Send a request. The second argument says who is asking.
const added = await mediator.send(new AddNote('Buy oat milk'), { actor: 'priya' });
const found = await mediator.send(new GetNote(added.id), { actor: 'priya' });
console.log(found?.title); // "Buy oat milk"
```

Running it prints:

```text
[mediator] AddNote ok (0.2ms)
[mediator] GetNote ok (0.0ms)
Buy oat milk
```

Three things to notice:

- **`send` is typed end to end.** `added` is a `Note` and `found` is a `Note | undefined`, taken from the
  class's type parameter. There is no casting and no string name to mistype.
- **The caller does not know the handler.** A route, a test, a scheduled job and a chat assistant all
  send the same `AddNote`. You can move, rewrite or split the handler without touching any of them.
- **The log line came from the pipeline.** Neither handler mentions logging. The next section is why
  that matters.

## Add locking and an audit trail without touching a handler

Shared steps are called **behaviors**. Each one wraps every request, so a rule written once applies
everywhere. Two come with the library:

- `MutexBehavior` stops two commands working on the same thing at the same time.
- `AuditBehavior` writes one record of who did what, whether it worked or failed.

A command opts in by adding a method. Nothing else changes:

```ts
import { AuditBehavior, Command, createMediator, LoggingBehavior, MutexBehavior, type AuditEntry } from '@garkpit/mediator';

class RenameNote extends Command<void> {
  constructor(readonly id: string, readonly title: string) {
    super();
  }
  // "Only one rename of this note at a time."
  mutexKey() {
    return `note:${this.id}`;
  }
  // "Record this change."
  auditInfo() {
    return { action: 'note.rename', resourceId: this.id, details: { title: this.title } };
  }
}

const auditLog: AuditEntry[] = [];

const mediator = createMediator({
  // Outermost first: take the lock, then audit, then log, then run the handler.
  behaviors: [
    new MutexBehavior(),
    new AuditBehavior({
      appendEntry: async (entry) => {
        auditLog.push(entry); // a real app inserts a database row here
      },
      mapError: () => ({ code: 'INTERNAL' })
    }),
    new LoggingBehavior()
  ]
});

mediator.register(RenameNote, { handle: async () => {} });
await mediator.send(new RenameNote('n1', 'Weekly shop'), { actor: 'priya' });
console.log(auditLog[0]?.action, auditLog[0]?.actor, auditLog[0]?.outcome); // note.rename priya ok
```

## See it all working

The repository has a small runnable app, [`examples/notes`](../examples/notes/README.md), with four
features, an HTTP door, a chat-assistant door and an MCP door, all sharing one pipeline:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/garkpit/GarkpitMediator.git
cd GarkpitMediator
bun install
bun run example
```

<!-- docs/commands-and-queries.md -->

# Commands and Queries

Every request your app handles is one of two things. A **Query** reads and returns data. A **Command**
changes something. The split is called CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation), and in this
library it is nothing more than two base classes and a habit: name each thing the app can do, and say
which kind it is.

## Writing a request class

A request is a class that extends `Query<R>` or `Command<R>`. `R` is the type its handler returns.
The constructor carries the inputs.

```ts
import { Command, Query } from '@garkpit/mediator';

interface Invoice {
  id: string;
  customer: string;
  totalPence: number;
  paid: boolean;
}

// Reads one invoice.
export class GetInvoice extends Query<Invoice> {
  constructor(readonly id: string) {
    super();
  }
}

// Reads many, with a filter.
export class ListInvoices extends Query<Invoice[]> {
  constructor(readonly filter: { customer?: string; unpaidOnly?: boolean } = {}) {
    super();
  }
}

// Changes one, and returns the new state.
export class MarkInvoicePaid extends Command<Invoice> {
  constructor(readonly id: string, readonly paidOn: Date) {
    super();
  }
}

// Changes something and returns nothing: Command's result type defaults to void.
export class SendInvoiceReminder extends Command {
  constructor(readonly id: string) {
    super();
  }
}
```

Good request classes share a few traits:

- **The name is verb then noun, and says what happens.** `MarkInvoicePaid`, not `InvoiceUpdate` or
  `HandleInvoice`. The list of class names should read like a description of the app.
- **The inputs are already valid.** Parse untyped input (a JSON body, a tool call) before you construct
  the request, so a handler never has to wonder whether `id` is really a string. A static `parse`
  method on the class is a tidy home for that; see [vertical slices](vertical-slices.md).
- **They hold data, not behaviour.** No database handles, no services. A request should be something
  you could print.
- **One name, once.** The mediator finds handlers by class name, so two request classes in one app
  cannot share a name. See the [FAQ](faq.md#why-are-handlers-keyed-by-class-name) for why.

## Writing a handler

A handler is any object with a `handle` method that takes the request and returns a promise of the
result. Use a class when the handler needs things (a database, a mail sender), so they arrive through
the constructor and tests can swap them:

```ts
import type { Handler } from '@garkpit/mediator';

interface InvoiceStore {
  find(id: string): Promise<Invoice | undefined>;
  save(invoice: Invoice): Promise<void>;
}

class InvoiceNotFoundError extends Error {}

export class GetInvoiceHandler implements Handler<GetInvoice, Invoice> {
  constructor(private readonly store: InvoiceStore) {}

  async handle(query: GetInvoice): Promise<Invoice> {
    const invoice = await this.store.find(query.id);
    if (!invoice) throw new InvoiceNotFoundError(`Invoice ${query.id} does not exist.`);
    return invoice;
  }
}

export class MarkInvoicePaidHandler implements Handler<MarkInvoicePaid, Invoice> {
  constructor(private readonly store: InvoiceStore) {}

  async handle(command: MarkInvoicePaid): Promise<Invoice> {
    const invoice = await this.store.find(command.id);
    if (!invoice) throw new InvoiceNotFoundError(`Invoice ${command.id} does not exist.`);
    const paid = { ...invoice, paid: true };
    await this.store.save(paid);
    return paid;
  }
}
```

A handler knows about the things it needs and nothing about how it was called. It never sees an HTTP
request, a cookie or a response. That is what lets the same handler serve a web page, a command-line
tool, a scheduled job and an AI agent.

## Registering and sending

```ts
import { createMediator, HandlerNotRegisteredError } from '@garkpit/mediator';

const mediator = createMediator();

mediator.register(GetInvoice, new GetInvoiceHandler(store));
mediator.register(MarkInvoicePaid, new MarkInvoicePaidHandler(store));

// The result type follows the request class: `invoice` is an Invoice.
const invoice = await mediator.send(new MarkInvoicePaid('inv-204', new Date()), { actor: 'omar' });
console.log(invoice.paid);

// The app can list what it is able to do.
console.log(mediator.registeredRequestTypes()); // ['GetInvoice', 'MarkInvoicePaid']
```

What can go wrong, and what you get:

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| You `send` a request nobody registered a handler for | `HandlerNotRegisteredError`, with the class name in `requestName` |
| You `register` a second handler for the same class name | `HandlerAlreadyRegisteredError` at start-up, not a silent overwrite |
| The handler throws | The same error reaches the caller, unchanged, after every behavior has seen it |

## The request context: who is asking

The second argument to `send` is the **request context**. It travels to every behavior. It has four
fields:

| Field | What it is for |
|---|---|
| `actor` | Who is making the request: a user id, a service name. Required. `AuditBehavior` records it. |
| `correlationId` | An id you choose (often one per HTTP request) so the audit row can be matched to your logs. |
| `audit` | Extra key/values for this one send's audit row, such as how the request arrived (`{ via: 'assistant-chat' }`). They can add to what the command reports but never overwrite it. |
| `secrets` | Values that must never appear in the audit row, wherever they turn up: a key someone typed into a form, say. Each is replaced with `[REDACTED]`. |

```ts
await mediator.send(new MarkInvoicePaid('inv-204', new Date()), {
  actor: 'omar',
  correlationId: crypto.randomUUID(),
  audit: { via: 'bulk-import', batch: '2026-11' }
});
```

Handlers do not receive the context. If a handler needs to know who is asking (to filter a list to the
caller's own records, say) put that on the request: `new ListInvoices({ ownerId: session.userId })`.
The context is for the pipeline; the request is for the handler.

## Should a Query ever change anything?

No. If reading has a side effect that matters (marking a message as read, counting a download) it is a
Command that happens to return data. Keeping Queries pure is what lets an AI assistant run them
without asking anyone, and lets you cache or retry them without thinking. See
[the agentic interface](agentic-interface.md).

## Where next

- [Behaviors](behaviors.md): locking, auditing and logging for every request.
- [The HTTP envelope](http.md): turning results and errors into JSON responses.

<!-- docs/behaviors.md -->

# Behaviors

A **behavior** is a step that wraps every request on its way to the handler and on its way back. It is
where you put the rules that would otherwise be copied into every endpoint: take a lock, write an audit
record, log a line, check a permission. Other frameworks call the same idea middleware.

![The request pipeline: send passes through each behavior, outermost first, reaches the one handler, and the result travels back out through the same behaviors in reverse.](images/pipeline.svg)

Behaviors run in the order you list them, outermost first. With `[mutex, audit, logging]`, a request
passes through the lock, then the audit step, then the logger, reaches the handler, and the result
travels back out through the logger, the audit step and the lock.

```ts
import { AuditBehavior, createMediator, LoggingBehavior, MutexBehavior } from '@garkpit/mediator';

// Build stateful behaviors once, where the app starts, and reuse them.
const mutex = new MutexBehavior();
const audit = new AuditBehavior({
  appendEntry: async (entry) => console.log('audit', entry.action, entry.outcome),
  mapError: () => ({ code: 'INTERNAL' })
});

export const mediator = createMediator({ behaviors: [mutex, audit, new LoggingBehavior()] });
```

**The order is a decision.** With the lock outermost, a command that is refused because the lock is
held never reaches the audit step, so a refusal leaves no audit row. Put `audit` first if you want
refused attempts recorded as failures.

## MutexBehavior: one at a time

A mutex (short for mutual exclusion) is a lock. `MutexBehavior` makes sure two commands that name the
same key never run at once. A command opts in by having a `mutexKey()` method:

```ts
import { Command, type HasMutexKey } from '@garkpit/mediator';

// One key: only one rename per note at a time. Renames of different notes run side by side.
export class RenameNote extends Command<void> implements HasMutexKey {
  constructor(readonly id: string, readonly title: string) {
    super();
  }
  mutexKey() {
    return `note:${this.id}`;
  }
}

// Several keys: all taken together, or none.
export class MoveNote extends Command<void> implements HasMutexKey {
  constructor(readonly noteId: string, readonly fromFolder: string, readonly toFolder: string) {
    super();
  }
  mutexKey() {
    return [`note:${this.noteId}`, `folder:${this.fromFolder}`, `folder:${this.toFolder}`];
  }
}
```

How it behaves:

- **It fails fast; it does not queue.** If a key is held, the second command is rejected at once with
  `MutexHeldError` (its `key` property says which). The caller decides whether to retry. A web route
  usually answers `409`.
- **Several keys are all-or-nothing.** If any one is held, none is taken, so nothing is left half
  locked. Keys are sorted before they are taken, which rules out two commands each waiting for the
  other.
- **Locks are always released,** whether the handler returns or throws.
- **Requests without `mutexKey()` pass straight through.** Queries normally have none.
- **The locks live in this one process.** They are a set in memory inside the `MutexBehavior` instance.
  They do not coordinate across several servers or across restarts. Build one instance at start-up and
  give that same instance to every mediator you create. If you run more than one server process and
  need a lock they all respect, write a behavior that takes it from your database or Redis; the
  interface is the same.

## AuditBehavior: who did what

`AuditBehavior` writes one record for every request that has an `auditInfo()` method: one row when it
succeeds, one row when it fails. You supply the function that stores the row.

```ts
import { AuditBehavior, Command, MutexHeldError, type AuditEntry, type AuditInfo, type HasAuditInfo } from '@garkpit/mediator';

export class DeleteNote extends Command<void> implements HasAuditInfo {
  constructor(readonly id: string, readonly reason: string) {
    super();
  }
  auditInfo(): AuditInfo {
    return { action: 'note.delete', resourceId: this.id, details: { reason: this.reason } };
  }
}

const rows: AuditEntry[] = [];

export const audit = new AuditBehavior({
  // Required: store one row. In a real app this is a database insert.
  appendEntry: async (entry) => {
    rows.push(entry);
  },
  // Required: turn any thrown error into a short code for the row.
  mapError: (error) => ({ code: error instanceof MutexHeldError ? 'MUTEX_HELD' : 'INTERNAL' })
});
```

Each row is an `AuditEntry`:

| Field | Contents |
|---|---|
| `id`, `timestamp` | A fresh UUID and the ISO time the row was built |
| `actor` | `ctx.actor`, or `'system'` when `send` was called without a context (change it with `defaultActor`) |
| `action`, `resourceId`, `details` | What the command reported in `auditInfo()` |
| `outcome` | `'ok'` or `'fail'` |
| `error` | On failure: `{ code, message }`, the code from your `mapError` |
| `commandName`, `durationMs` | The request class name and how long the handler took |
| `correlationId` | `ctx.correlationId`, when given |
| `schemaVersion` | `2`, so stored rows can be told apart if the shape ever changes |

Things worth knowing:

- **Auditing never changes the outcome.** If your `appendEntry` throws, the failure is reported (to
  `console.error`, or to your `reportFailure`) and the command's own result or error reaches the caller
  untouched.
- **Secrets are redacted before the row is stored.** Any value in `details` whose *key* looks secret
  (`token`, `password`, `api_key`, `authorization`, `cookie`, and similar) becomes `[REDACTED]`, four
  levels deep. Pass your own `redactSecrets` to change the rule. For secret *values* under innocent
  keys, pass them in `ctx.secrets` and they are scrubbed from the details and the error message
  wherever they appear.
- **`auditInfo()` is read after the handler runs.** A handler can set a field on the command first (the
  id of the thing it just created, a snapshot of what it deleted) and the row will include it.
- **A change that changed nothing is not recorded.** If `details.columnsPatched` is an empty array, no
  row is written. Use it for "save" buttons pressed with nothing edited.
- **Any request can be audited,** Queries included: give a sensitive read an `auditInfo()` and it gets
  a row.

### Your own audit fields

Apps often need an extra dimension on every row: which customer account, which workspace. Extend
`AuditInfo`, and your writer receives the command's own info next to the entry:

```ts
import { AuditBehavior, Command, type AuditInfo, type HasAuditInfo } from '@garkpit/mediator';

interface WorkspaceAuditInfo extends AuditInfo {
  workspace: string;
}

export class ArchiveProject extends Command<void> implements HasAuditInfo<WorkspaceAuditInfo> {
  constructor(readonly workspace: string, readonly projectId: string) {
    super();
  }
  auditInfo(): WorkspaceAuditInfo {
    return { action: 'project.archive', workspace: this.workspace, resourceId: this.projectId, details: {} };
  }
}

declare function insertAuditRow(row: object): Promise<void>;

export const audit = new AuditBehavior<WorkspaceAuditInfo>({
  appendEntry: async (entry, info) => insertAuditRow({ ...entry, workspace: info.workspace }),
  mapError: () => ({ code: 'INTERNAL' })
});
```

### Mirroring into a general log

If you also keep one general application log, pass `appendLogEntry` and `logSource` and each audit row
is copied into it as a `LogEntry` (the function `auditEntryToLogEntry` does the conversion, and is
exported if you want it elsewhere).

## LoggingBehavior: one line per request

```ts
import { createMediator, LoggingBehavior } from '@garkpit/mediator';

// Default: console.log
const quick = createMediator({ behaviors: [new LoggingBehavior()] });

// Or send the lines wherever you like. `error` is set when the request failed.
const lines: string[] = [];
const collected = createMediator({
  behaviors: [new LoggingBehavior((line, error) => lines.push(error ? `${line} ${String(error)}` : line))]
});
```

It prints `[mediator] RenameNote ok (1.2ms)` on success and `[mediator] RenameNote FAIL (0.4ms):`
followed by the error on failure, then passes the error on unchanged.

## Writing your own

A behavior is a class with one method, `invoke(request, next, ctx)`. Call `next()` to carry on down the
pipeline. Do work before it, after it, or instead of it.

**Do something around every request:**

```ts
import type { Next, PipelineBehavior, Request, RequestContext } from '@garkpit/mediator';

/** Warns when any request takes longer than its budget. */
export class SlowRequestBehavior implements PipelineBehavior {
  constructor(private readonly budgetMs: number) {}

  async invoke<TRequest extends Request<TResponse>, TResponse>(
    request: TRequest,
    next: Next<TResponse>,
    ctx?: RequestContext
  ): Promise<TResponse> {
    const started = performance.now();
    try {
      return await next();
    } finally {
      const took = performance.now() - started;
      if (took > this.budgetMs) {
        console.warn(`${request.constructor.name} took ${took.toFixed(0)}ms for ${ctx?.actor ?? 'unknown'}`);
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**Stop a request before it reaches the handler.** The built-in behaviors use a small pattern you can
copy: the request opts in with a method, and the behavior checks for that method.

```ts
import type { Next, PipelineBehavior, Request, RequestContext } from '@garkpit/mediator';

/** A request that needs a role implements this. */
export interface RequiresRole {
  requiredRole(): string;
}

function requiresRole(request: unknown): request is RequiresRole {
  return typeof request === 'object' && request !== null && typeof (request as RequiresRole).requiredRole === 'function';
}

export class ForbiddenError extends Error {}

export class PermissionBehavior implements PipelineBehavior {
  constructor(private readonly rolesOf: (actor: string) => Promise<readonly string[]>) {}

  async invoke<TRequest extends Request<TResponse>, TResponse>(
    request: TRequest,
    next: Next<TResponse>,
    ctx?: RequestContext
  ): Promise<TResponse> {
    if (requiresRole(request)) {
      const roles = ctx ? await this.rolesOf(ctx.actor) : [];
      if (!roles.includes(request.requiredRole())) {
        throw new ForbiddenError(`${request.constructor.name} needs the "${request.requiredRole()}" role.`);
      }
    }
    return next();
  }
}
```

Now a permission rule is one method on a command (`requiredRole() { return 'admin'; }`), it is enforced
for every caller including AI agents, and nobody can forget to add the check to a new endpoint.

Rules for behaviors:

- **Write them as classes.** The mediator tells behaviors apart by class name and allows each class
  once per mediator; a second `use` of the same class throws `BehaviorAlreadyRegisteredError`. Two
  plain object literals would both be named `Object` and collide.
- **Add them with `createMediator({ behaviors })` or `mediator.use(behavior)`.** Both append, so the
  first one added is the outermost.
- **Keep state that must outlive a request in the behavior instance,** and build that instance once.
- **Do not swallow errors.** Let them travel back out so the behaviors around you, and the caller, see
  them.

## Where next

- [The HTTP envelope](http.md): the JSON shape for results and errors.
- [API reference](api-reference.md): every option of every behavior.

<!-- docs/http.md -->

# The HTTP envelope and body limits

The mediator itself knows nothing about HTTP. A separate entry point, `@garkpit/mediator/http`, has
three small helpers for the routes that sit in front of it:

- `ok` and `fail` build JSON responses in one fixed shape, so every client and every agent can tell
  success from failure the same way.
- `readBoundedBody` reads a request body but refuses one that is too large.

They use the standard `Request` and `Response` objects, so they work in Bun, SvelteKit, Hono, Deno and
any other runtime built on the Fetch API. They are kept out of the main entry point so a browser bundle
never pulls them in by accident.

## One shape for every response

Every response is one of two JSON shapes, called the **envelope**:

```json
{ "ok": true, "data": { "id": "n1", "title": "Shopping" } }
```

```json
{ "ok": false, "error": { "code": "NOT_FOUND", "message": "Note n404 does not exist." } }
```

```ts
import { fail, ok } from '@garkpit/mediator/http';

// 200 with {"ok":true,"data":{...}}
const found = ok({ id: 'n1', title: 'Shopping' });

// Another success status, or extra headers
const created = ok({ id: 'n2' }, { status: 201, headers: { location: '/notes/n2' } });

// The status comes from the code: NOT_FOUND is 404
const missing = fail({ code: 'NOT_FOUND', message: 'Note n404 does not exist.' });

// `details` is yours: field errors, the key that was locked, anything the client can use
const invalid = fail({ code: 'VALIDATION_FAILED', message: 'Title is required.', details: { field: 'title' } });

console.log(found.status, created.status, missing.status, invalid.status); // 200 201 404 400
```

Both set `content-type: application/json` and an exact `content-length`.

### Error codes and statuses

`fail` looks the status up from the error code:

| Code | Status |
|---|---|
| `VALIDATION_FAILED` | 400 |
| `UNAUTHORIZED` | 401 |
| `NOT_FOUND` | 404 |
| `CONFLICT` | 409 |
| `MUTEX_HELD` | 409 |
| `PRECONDITION_FAILED` | 412 |
| `INTERNAL` | 500 |
| `UPSTREAM_FAILED` | 502 |
| anything else | 500 |

Add your own codes by extending the table and passing it in. Or set one status directly:

```ts
import { DEFAULT_STATUS_FOR_CODE, fail, statusForCode } from '@garkpit/mediator/http';

const STATUS_FOR_CODE = { ...DEFAULT_STATUS_FOR_CODE, PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE: 413, RATE_LIMITED: 429 };

const tooBig = fail({ code: 'PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE', message: 'That file is over the 2 MB limit.' }, { table: STATUS_FOR_CODE });
const teapot = fail({ code: 'INTERNAL', message: 'Short and stout.' }, { statusOverride: 418 });

console.log(tooBig.status, teapot.status, statusForCode('RATE_LIMITED', STATUS_FOR_CODE)); // 413 418 429
```

## A complete route

A route has three jobs: turn the HTTP request into a Command or Query, send it, and wrap what comes
back. Mapping errors to codes belongs in one function that every route shares.

```ts
import { MutexHeldError } from '@garkpit/mediator';
import { fail, ok, readBoundedBody, RequestBodyLimitError, type ApiErrorShape } from '@garkpit/mediator/http';

// One place that knows how errors become codes.
function toApiError(error: unknown): ApiErrorShape {
  if (error instanceof ValidationError) return { code: 'VALIDATION_FAILED', message: error.message };
  if (error instanceof NotFoundError) return { code: 'NOT_FOUND', message: error.message };
  if (error instanceof MutexHeldError) return { code: 'MUTEX_HELD', message: 'Someone else is changing this. Try again.' };
  if (error instanceof RequestBodyLimitError) return { code: 'VALIDATION_FAILED', message: error.message };
  return { code: 'INTERNAL', message: 'Something went wrong.' }; // never leak internals
}

// PATCH /notes/:id
export async function renameNoteRoute(request: Request, noteId: string, userId: string): Promise<Response> {
  try {
    const bytes = await readBoundedBody(request, 16 * 1024);
    const body = JSON.parse(new TextDecoder().decode(bytes)) as { title?: unknown };
    if (typeof body.title !== 'string' || body.title === '') throw new ValidationError('"title" must be a non-empty string.');

    const note = await mediator.send(new RenameNote(noteId, body.title), { actor: userId });
    return ok(note);
  } catch (error) {
    return fail(toApiError(error));
  }
}
```

In SvelteKit the same route is a `+server.ts` file. This is a sketch (it is not compiled by this
repository's checks, because the library does not depend on SvelteKit):

```ts nocheck
// src/routes/api/notes/[id]/+server.ts
import type { RequestHandler } from './$types';
import { fail, ok, readBoundedBody } from '@garkpit/mediator/http';
import { mediator } from '$lib/server/mediator';
import { toApiError } from '$lib/server/errors';
import { RenameNote } from '$lib/features/notes/rename-note/RenameNote';

export const PATCH: RequestHandler = async ({ request, params, locals }) => {
  try {
    const bytes = await readBoundedBody(request, 16 * 1024);
    const command = RenameNote.parse({ ...JSON.parse(new TextDecoder().decode(bytes)), id: params.id });
    return ok(await mediator.send(command, { actor: locals.user.id }));
  } catch (error) {
    return fail(toApiError(error));
  }
};
```

## Reading a body with a limit

`readBoundedBody(request, limit)` returns the body as bytes, and protects you from a client that sends
far more than you expect:

- If the request declares a `content-length` over the limit, it is refused before a single byte is
  read.
- If the body is streamed with no declared length, reading stops and the stream is cancelled the
  moment it passes the limit.
- A request with no body gives an empty array.

Either refusal throws `RequestBodyLimitError`, which carries the `limit` and, when the client declared
one, the `declared` size.

```ts
import { readBoundedBody, RequestBodyLimitError } from '@garkpit/mediator/http';

const request = new Request('https://example.test/upload', { method: 'POST', body: 'x'.repeat(5000) });

try {
  await readBoundedBody(request, 1024);
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof RequestBodyLimitError) {
    console.log(error.message, error.limit); // "Request body exceeds the 1024-byte limit." 1024
  }
}
```

## On the client

Because the shape never varies, one small function unwraps every call:

```ts
type Envelope<T> =
  | { ok: true; data: T }
  | { ok: false; error: { code: string; message: string; details?: unknown } };

export class ApiError extends Error {
  constructor(readonly code: string, message: string, readonly details?: unknown) {
    super(message);
  }
}

export async function api<T>(path: string, init?: RequestInit): Promise<T> {
  const response = await fetch(path, init);
  const body = (await response.json()) as Envelope<T>;
  if (!body.ok) throw new ApiError(body.error.code, body.error.message, body.error.details);
  return body.data;
}
```

## Where next

- [Growing an app with vertical slices](vertical-slices.md): where routes, requests and handlers live.
- [`examples/notes`](../examples/notes/README.md): a runnable app whose routes all follow this page.

<!-- docs/vertical-slices.md -->

# Growing an app with vertical slices

Most codebases start tidy and get harder to change as they grow. The usual cause is not bad code. It
is that one feature ends up spread across a routes folder, a services folder, a models folder and a
utils folder, so every change means finding and editing four files that also serve twenty other
features.

A **vertical slice** is the opposite arrangement: one folder per feature, holding everything that
feature needs. The mediator is what makes it practical, because a feature is then exactly one request
class and one handler.

## The layout

```tree
src/
  app.ts                          builds the mediator and its behaviors, registers every feature
  errors.ts                       typed errors, and the one function that maps them to error codes
  features/
    notes/
      index.ts                    one registration line per slice
      create-note/
        CreateNote.ts             the Command: its inputs, its lock key, its audit record
        CreateNoteHandler.ts      the only code that creates a note
        CreateNote.test.ts        sends CreateNote through the real pipeline
      rename-note/
        RenameNote.ts
        RenameNoteHandler.ts
        RenameNote.test.ts
      get-note/
        GetNote.ts                a Query
        GetNoteHandler.ts
        GetNote.test.ts
    billing/
      index.ts
      mark-invoice-paid/
        ...
  http/
    routes.ts                     thin: parse, send, wrap in ok/fail
```

This is the real layout of [`examples/notes`](../examples/notes/README.md). Open any slice there and
you will find these three files.

## The three files of a slice

**The request** says what the feature is, what it needs, and which shared rules apply to it.

```ts
// features/notes/rename-note/RenameNote.ts
import { Command, type AuditInfo, type HasAuditInfo, type HasMutexKey } from '@garkpit/mediator';

export interface Note {
  id: string;
  title: string;
}

export class RenameNote extends Command<Note> implements HasMutexKey, HasAuditInfo {
  constructor(readonly id: string, readonly title: string) {
    super();
  }

  mutexKey(): string {
    return `note:${this.id}`;
  }

  auditInfo(): AuditInfo {
    return { action: 'note.rename', resourceId: this.id, details: { title: this.title } };
  }

  /** The one place untyped input becomes a RenameNote. Routes and agent tools both call it. */
  static parse(input: unknown): RenameNote {
    const { id, title } = (input ?? {}) as { id?: unknown; title?: unknown };
    if (typeof id !== 'string' || id === '') throw new Error('"id" must be a non-empty string.');
    if (typeof title !== 'string' || title.trim() === '') throw new Error('"title" must be a non-empty string.');
    return new RenameNote(id, title.trim());
  }
}
```

**The handler** does the work, and is the only place that does.

```ts
// features/notes/rename-note/RenameNoteHandler.ts
import type { Handler } from '@garkpit/mediator';

export interface NotesStore {
  update(id: string, changes: { title: string }): Promise<Note | undefined>;
}

export class RenameNoteHandler implements Handler<RenameNote, Note> {
  constructor(private readonly store: NotesStore) {}

  async handle(command: RenameNote): Promise<Note> {
    const note = await this.store.update(command.id, { title: command.title });
    if (!note) throw new Error(`Note ${command.id} does not exist.`);
    return note;
  }
}
```

**The test** sends the request through the real mediator, behaviors included, so it proves what a real
caller would see.

```ts nocheck
// features/notes/rename-note/RenameNote.test.ts
import { expect, test } from 'bun:test';
import { createApp } from '../../../app';
import { CreateNote } from '../create-note/CreateNote';
import { RenameNote } from './RenameNote';

test('RenameNote renames the note and audits the change', async () => {
  const app = createApp();
  const { id } = await app.mediator.send(new CreateNote('Draft', ''), { actor: 'priya' });

  expect(await app.mediator.send(new RenameNote(id, 'Final'), { actor: 'priya' })).toMatchObject({ id, title: 'Final' });
  expect(app.auditLog.at(-1)).toMatchObject({ action: 'note.rename', outcome: 'ok', resourceId: id });
});
```

Registration is one line per slice, in the feature area's `index.ts`:

```ts
// features/notes/index.ts
import type { MediatorPort } from '@garkpit/mediator';

export function registerNotes(mediator: MediatorPort, store: NotesStore): void {
  mediator.register(CreateNote, new CreateNoteHandler(store));
  mediator.register(RenameNote, new RenameNoteHandler(store));
  mediator.register(GetNote, new GetNoteHandler(store));
}
```

## The rules that keep it tidy

1. **Dependencies point inward.** Routes know the mediator and the request classes. Handlers know the
   things they are given (a store, a mail sender). Nothing inner imports anything outer: a handler
   never sees an HTTP request, and a route never touches the database.
2. **A slice does one thing, and its name says what.** When a handler starts doing a second thing,
   that is a second slice.
3. **Slices do not call each other's handlers.** If two slices need the same logic, move it into a
   plain function both import. If one feature must trigger another, the caller (a route, a job) sends
   two requests.
4. **Shared rules live in behaviors, never in handlers.** No handler takes a lock, writes an audit row
   or logs its own timing.
5. **Routes are thin.** Parse, send, wrap. If a route has an `if` about business rules, the rule
   belongs in a handler.

## What a change touches

This is the point of the whole arrangement. As the app doubles in size, the cost of one change stays
the same:

| You want to | You touch |
|---|---|
| Add a feature | One new folder (three files), one registration line, usually one route |
| Change how a feature works | That feature's handler and its test |
| Find where something happens | The folder named after it |
| Add a rule to every feature (permissions, rate limits) | One new behavior, added in one place |
| Delete a feature | Its folder, its registration line, its route |
| Give an AI agent access to a feature | One catalogue entry: see [the agentic interface](agentic-interface.md) |

Nothing in that table grows with the number of features you already have.

## Keep a list you can trust

`mediator.registeredRequestTypes()` returns the name of every request that has a handler. Use it to
keep promises about the whole app in a test, for instance "every Command is audited" or "every request
has an entry in the assistant's tool catalogue". A test like that fails the moment someone adds a
feature and forgets the other half.

```ts
// Every registered request has a catalogue entry, and the other way round.
expect(catalogue.map((tool) => tool.name).sort()).toEqual([...mediator.registeredRequestTypes()]);
```

## Where next

- [Working with AI coding agents](ai-coding-agents.md): why this layout suits them, and the snippet
  that teaches them to keep it.
- [The agentic interface](agentic-interface.md): turning the list of slices into tools.

---

<!-- docs/ai-coding-agents.md -->

# Working with AI coding agents

An AI coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and the like) is a fast, capable programmer that starts
every task knowing nothing about your project. It reads a few files, forms a picture, and writes code
that fits the picture. Whether that goes well depends far more on the shape of your codebase than on
the model.

## Why a mediator helps

**There is one obvious place for each thing.** Ask an agent to "let users archive a note" in a typical
app and it has to guess: a new route file, or the existing one? Logic in the route, or a service? Which
of the three existing patterns should it copy? Each guess is a chance to drift. In a mediator app the
answer is always the same: a new folder with a request class, a handler and a test. The agent copies
the folder next door.

**The app can be listed.** The feature folders, and `mediator.registeredRequestTypes()`, are a complete
inventory of what the app does. An agent can read that list in seconds instead of inferring features
from a tangle of routes. Finding the code to change becomes a lookup, not a search.

**Shared rules cannot be forgotten.** Locking, auditing, logging and permission checks live in
behaviors that wrap every request. The agent does not need to remember to add them to a new endpoint,
so it cannot forget.

**Small files, small context.** A slice is three short files. The agent reads only those to change a
feature, which leaves more of its working memory for the task and less for reading unrelated code.

**The compiler checks the wiring.** `send` returns the type the request class declares, so a wrong
result type or a missing field is a compile error the agent sees and fixes itself.

None of this is specific to one model or tool. It is the same thing that helps a new human colleague,
which is the point: agents do well in codebases where people do well.

## The snippet for your AGENTS.md

`AGENTS.md` is the file most coding agents read first in a repository (Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md`;
the content is the same). Paste this into yours and adjust the paths to match your project:

```md
## Features go through the mediator

This app uses `@garkpit/mediator` (copied into `packages/mediator`; the full manual is
`packages/mediator/llms-full.txt`). Every feature is one Command (it changes something) or one Query
(it only reads), and each has exactly one handler.

To add or change a feature:

1. Look first. Each feature is a folder at `src/features/<area>/<verb-noun>/`. List them and reuse or
   extend an existing one before creating a new one.
2. A new feature is a new folder with three files. Copy the nearest existing slice and rename:
   - `VerbNoun.ts`: the request class. It `extends Command<Result>` or `extends Query<Result>`, its
     constructor takes typed, already-valid values, and a static `parse(input: unknown)` validates
     untyped input.
   - `VerbNounHandler.ts`: `implements Handler<VerbNoun, Result>`. All the logic lives here. It never
     touches the HTTP request or response.
   - `VerbNoun.test.ts`: sends the request through the real mediator and checks the result.
3. Register it with one line in the area's `index.ts`:
   `mediator.register(VerbNoun, new VerbNounHandler(deps))`.
4. Keep routes thin: parse the input, `mediator.send(request, { actor })`, then `ok(data)` or
   `fail(error)`. A route holds no business logic and never touches the database.

Rules:

- Never call a handler directly, and never call one handler from another. Send a request, or move the
  shared code into a plain function that both handlers import.
- Never write locking, audit or logging code in a handler. A command that must not run twice at once on
  the same thing implements `mutexKey()`. A command that should leave a record implements
  `auditInfo()`. The pipeline does the rest.
- Request class names are unique across the app: the mediator finds handlers by class name.
- Every `send` passes `{ actor }` as its second argument.
- Handlers throw typed errors. One shared function maps errors to error codes; do not map them inside
  a route.
- A Query never changes anything. If it does, it is a Command.
- Run `bun run check` before saying the work is done.
```

The same text is a file in the repository,
[`docs/snippets/AGENTS.md`](snippets/AGENTS.md), so you can fetch it from a script.

## The manual, in a form agents can read

Two plain-text files follow the [llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org) convention, a simple way of giving a
language model a project's documentation without the web page around it:

- [`llms.txt`](../llms.txt): a short index of these guides with one line about each.
- [`llms-full.txt`](../llms-full.txt): every guide joined into one file. Give an agent this and it has
  the whole manual.

Both are generated from these Markdown guides and checked on every `bun run check`, so they cannot
fall behind. `llms-full.txt` is one of the files the [install step](getting-started.md#install-copy-it-in)
copies into your project, which is why the snippet above can point at
`packages/mediator/llms-full.txt`.

## Prompts that work well

Because features have names, you can use them:

- "Add an `ArchiveNote` command next to `RenameNote`. Lock on the note. Audit it."
- "`ListInvoices` should accept an `unpaidOnly` filter. Update the handler and its test."
- "List every Command that has no `auditInfo()`."
- "Write a behavior that rejects any Command whose actor is `anonymous`, and add it outermost."

Each of those names a single, findable place. Compare "make archiving work", which sends the agent
exploring.

## Reviewing what an agent wrote

A slice is quick to review because there are few ways for it to be wrong:

- Is the new folder under the right feature area, with a request, a handler and a test?
- Does the request class name say what happens, and is it unique?
- Does a Command that touches shared data have a `mutexKey()`? Should it have an `auditInfo()`?
- Is there any logic in the route that belongs in the handler?
- Does the test send the request through the mediator, not call the handler directly?
- Is it registered?

## What this does not do

It does not make a model smarter, and it will not stop an agent writing a poor handler. What it does is
narrow where the agent has to look and where its code has to go, and that removes the most common way
agent-written code goes wrong in a large project: a reasonable change, put in the wrong place, in a
slightly different style from everything around it.

## Where next

- [The agentic interface](agentic-interface.md): letting AI agents *use* your app, not just write it.
- [Growing an app with vertical slices](vertical-slices.md): the layout the snippet assumes.

---

<!-- docs/agentic-interface.md -->

# The agentic interface: an app that AI can read and operate

An app built on the mediator has an unusual property: everything it can do is already a list of named,
typed requests. That is almost exactly what an AI model needs in order to use a tool: a name, a
description and the inputs. So with a small amount of extra code the app gains two new doors beside
its web pages:

- a **chat door**: an assistant inside the app that can look things up and propose changes on a
  person's behalf;
- an **MCP door**: an endpoint that outside AI agents (Claude, Codex, your own) can connect to. MCP is
  the Model Context Protocol, an open standard for giving AI applications tools to call.

Both doors send the same Commands and Queries, through the same locks, audit trail and logging, as a
button on a page does.

![Three doors, one pipeline: web pages, a chat assistant and outside agents over MCP all send the same Commands and Queries through the mediator's behaviors to the handlers.](images/doors.svg)

## What "self-aware" and "self-maintaining" mean here

These are big words, so here is exactly what is meant by them and what is not.

**Self-aware** means the app can describe what it can do. `mediator.registeredRequestTypes()` lists
every capability by name, and a catalogue adds a sentence and an input schema for each. An agent that
connects does not have to be told what is possible, and does not have to scrape pages to find out. It
asks.

**Self-maintaining** means agents can safely run the app's day-to-day operations, because every action
they take goes through the one audited, locked door that people use. An agent cannot skip a permission
check or forget the audit row, because those are not its to skip: they are in the pipeline. And when a
coding agent adds a feature, the new Command is one catalogue entry away from being usable by every
other agent.

It does **not** mean the app rewrites itself, fixes its own bugs unattended, or needs no people. People
still decide what gets built and confirm what gets changed.

## Step 1: a tool catalogue

A catalogue is a list with one entry per request: its class, a description a model can read, and a
schema for its inputs. Each entry builds its request with the same `parse` function the HTTP route
uses, so there is one set of validation rules, not two.

```ts
import { Command as BaseCommand, type Request as MediatorRequest } from '@garkpit/mediator';

export interface Tool {
  /** The request class name: the same string the mediator keys handlers by. */
  name: string;
  /** Queries only read. Commands change something. */
  kind: 'query' | 'command';
  description: string;
  /** A JSON Schema for the input object. */
  inputSchema: { type: 'object'; properties: Record<string, { type: string; description: string }>; required: string[] };
  /** Untyped input in, validated request out. */
  build(input: unknown): MediatorRequest<unknown>;
}

interface RequestClass {
  name: string;
  prototype: MediatorRequest<unknown>;
  parse(input: unknown): MediatorRequest<unknown>;
}

function tool(request: RequestClass, description: string, fields: Record<string, string>): Tool {
  return {
    name: request.name,
    // Taken from the class, so it cannot disagree with the code.
    kind: request.prototype instanceof BaseCommand ? 'command' : 'query',
    description,
    inputSchema: {
      type: 'object',
      properties: Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(fields).map(([field, text]) => [field, { type: 'string', description: text }])),
      required: Object.keys(fields)
    },
    build: (input) => request.parse(input)
  };
}

export const catalogue: readonly Tool[] = [
  tool(GetNote, 'Read one note by its id.', { id: 'The note id, for example "n1".' }),
  tool(RenameNote, 'Change the title of an existing note.', { id: 'The note id.', title: 'The new title.' })
];
```

## Step 2: prove nothing is missing

One test keeps the catalogue honest. It fails when someone adds a feature without a tool, or leaves a
tool behind after deleting a feature:

```ts nocheck
test('the catalogue lists exactly the requests the mediator has handlers for', () => {
  expect(catalogue.map((tool) => tool.name).sort()).toEqual([...mediator.registeredRequestTypes()]);
});
```

If some requests should stay private to the app, keep a short written list of exclusions and subtract
it. The point is that leaving one out becomes a decision, not an accident.

## Step 3: the chat door

A chat model that supports tool calling is given the catalogue as its tools. When it calls one, the
call arrives at a small class that applies one rule: **reads run, changes wait for a person.**

```ts
import type { MediatorPort, RequestContext } from '@garkpit/mediator';

export type ToolOutcome =
  | { status: 'done'; data: unknown }
  | { status: 'needs-confirmation'; proposalId: string; tool: string; input: unknown };

export class AssistantDoor {
  private readonly pending = new Map<string, MediatorRequest<unknown>>();

  constructor(private readonly mediator: MediatorPort) {}

  /** One tool call from the model. */
  async call(name: string, input: unknown, ctx: RequestContext): Promise<ToolOutcome> {
    const tool = catalogue.find((t) => t.name === name);
    if (!tool) throw new Error(`There is no tool called "${name}".`);
    const request = tool.build(input); // validated now, before anyone is asked to confirm

    if (tool.kind === 'query') {
      return { status: 'done', data: await this.mediator.send(request, { ...ctx, audit: { via: 'assistant-chat' } }) };
    }
    const proposalId = crypto.randomUUID();
    this.pending.set(proposalId, request);
    return { status: 'needs-confirmation', proposalId, tool: name, input };
  }

  /** The person pressed Confirm. `ctx.actor` is that person. */
  async confirm(proposalId: string, ctx: RequestContext): Promise<unknown> {
    const request = this.pending.get(proposalId);
    if (!request) throw new Error('That proposal does not exist or was already decided.');
    this.pending.delete(proposalId);
    return this.mediator.send(request, { ...ctx, audit: { via: 'assistant-chat', proposalId } });
  }
}
```

What this gives you:

- The assistant can answer "which invoices are unpaid?" at once, because Queries change nothing.
- When it wants to change something it shows the person exactly what it proposes ("Rename note n1 to
  *Weekly shop*") and nothing happens until they agree.
- The confirmed command is recorded as the person's action, with `via: 'assistant-chat'` and the
  proposal id in the audit row's details, so you can always tell which changes arrived through the
  assistant.
- The command still takes its lock and passes every behavior. The assistant has no back door.

The class has no model in it on purpose. Connecting one is a few lines with whichever AI provider you
use: pass `catalogue` as the tool definitions, and route each tool call the model makes to
`door.call(...)`.

## Step 4: the MCP door

For agents outside your app, MCP needs two things from a server: a list of tools and a way to call one.
Both are short when you have a catalogue:

```ts
import type { MediatorPort, RequestContext } from '@garkpit/mediator';

export function listTools() {
  return catalogue.map((tool) => ({
    name: tool.name,
    description: tool.description,
    inputSchema: tool.inputSchema,
    annotations: { readOnlyHint: tool.kind === 'query' } // tells the client which tools only read
  }));
}

export async function callTool(mediator: MediatorPort, name: string, input: unknown, ctx: RequestContext) {
  const tool = catalogue.find((t) => t.name === name);
  if (!tool) return { content: [{ type: 'text', text: `There is no tool called "${name}".` }], isError: true };
  try {
    const data = await mediator.send(tool.build(input), { ...ctx, audit: { via: 'mcp' } });
    return { content: [{ type: 'text', text: JSON.stringify(data, null, 2) }] };
  } catch (error) {
    return { content: [{ type: 'text', text: error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error) }], isError: true };
  }
}
```

**This is a sketch of the two functions that matter, not a complete MCP server.** A real one also
handles the protocol's handshake, its transports and, above all, authentication, and for those you
should use the official MCP SDK for your language and call these two functions from its handlers.

[`examples/notes`](../examples/notes/README.md) goes one step further so you can try it: it wraps the
two functions in a minimal JSON-RPC handler (`src/agent/mcp.ts`), served both on standard input and
output and at `POST /mcp`. On 22 November 2026 that example was checked against the official MCP
TypeScript SDK client, version 1.32.2, over both transports: the client listed the four tools, created
a note and received a clean error for a missing one. It has no authentication and no sessions, and it
binds to your own machine only. Treat it as a demonstration.

## What the library provides for this

Nothing above needs a special "AI mode". These parts of the ordinary API are what make it short:

| Part | Role in an agentic interface |
|---|---|
| `Command` and `Query` | The read/write split tells a door which calls are safe to run unasked. |
| `registeredRequestTypes()` | The list a parity test compares the catalogue against. |
| `RequestContext.audit` | Records how a request arrived (`via`, a proposal id) without the Command knowing or caring. |
| `RequestContext.secrets` | Keeps a value a person typed for a tool (an API key, say) out of the audit row, whatever field it lands in. |
| `MediatorPort` | The small interface a door depends on, so the same door code works with any mediator of that shape. |
| Behaviors | Locks, audit and your permission rules apply to agents exactly as they apply to people. |

## Before you open a door

- **Decide who the actor is.** For the chat door it is the signed-in person. For MCP it is whoever the
  connection authenticated as. Never let a caller name its own actor.
- **Put permission checks in a behavior,** not in the door, so they hold for every way in.
- **Keep Queries pure.** A "read" that changes something would run without confirmation.
- **Think about what a Query can reveal.** Running unasked is fine for "list my notes" and wrong for
  "list every customer's card details". Give sensitive reads an `auditInfo()`, a permission rule, or
  leave them out of the catalogue.
- **Do not expose an unauthenticated MCP endpoint beyond your own machine.**

## Aires: the companion library

Everything on this page you can build yourself, and the example app does it in a few hundred lines. We
also use a fuller version of the same idea: **Aires**, our in-house companion library for apps built on
this mediator. It generates both doors from an app's Commands and Queries: an in-app chat assistant in
which every change is a proposal a person confirms, and an MCP endpoint for outside agents, with a
check that fails when a feature has no matching tool.

Aires is not yet public. Until it is, the pattern on this page and the code in
[`examples/notes`](../examples/notes/README.md) are the way to get the same shape in your own app, and
an app built this way will be ready for Aires without restructuring, because the hard part (every
capability as a named, typed request) is already done.

## Where next

- [`examples/notes`](../examples/notes/README.md): run `bun run example` and watch a person, an
  assistant and an MCP client change the same data through one pipeline.
- [Behaviors](behaviors.md): where to put the permission rules a door relies on.

---

<!-- docs/api-reference.md -->

# API reference

Everything the library exports, grouped by what you use it for. There are two entry points:

- `@garkpit/mediator`: requests, the mediator, behaviors and their types.
- `@garkpit/mediator/http`: the JSON envelope and the bounded body reader. Kept separate so browser
  code never pulls it in by accident.

This page is checked against the source on every `bun run check`: every exported name must appear here,
and every heading here must be a real export.

## Requests and handlers

### `Request`

```ts nocheck
abstract class Request<TResponse = void>
```

The base of every request. `TResponse` is the type the handler returns, and what `send` resolves to.
You normally extend `Command` or `Query`, not this. If you import it by name alongside HTTP code,
rename it (`import type { Request as MediatorRequest }`) so it does not hide the Fetch API's `Request`.

### `Command`

```ts nocheck
abstract class Command<TResponse = void> extends Request<TResponse>
```

A request that changes something. The result type defaults to `void`.

### `Query`

```ts nocheck
abstract class Query<TResponse> extends Request<TResponse>
```

A request that only reads. The result type is required.

### `Handler`

```ts nocheck
interface Handler<TRequest extends Request<TResponse>, TResponse> {
  handle(request: TRequest): Promise<TResponse>;
}
```

The code that carries out one kind of request. Any object with a matching `handle` method will do.

### `RequestConstructor`

```ts nocheck
type RequestConstructor<T extends Request<unknown>> = new (...args: never[]) => T;
```

The type of a request class itself, as taken by `register`.

### `RequestContext`

```ts nocheck
interface RequestContext {
  actor: string;
  readonly correlationId?: string;
  readonly audit?: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>;
  readonly secrets?: readonly string[];
}
```

Who is asking, passed as the second argument of `send` and handed to every behavior.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `actor` | Who is making the request. `AuditBehavior` records it. |
| `correlationId` | Your id for tying the audit row to other logs. |
| `audit` | Extra key/values merged into this send's audit `details`. They never overwrite a key the command itself reports. |
| `secrets` | Strings that must not appear anywhere in this send's audit row. Each is replaced with `[REDACTED]` in the details (keys and values) and in the error message. Empty strings are ignored. |

## The mediator

### `createMediator`

```ts nocheck
function createMediator(options?: CreateMediatorOptions): Mediator
```

Builds a `Mediator` and installs `options.behaviors` in order, outermost first. It holds no state of its
own: build stateful behaviors once and pass the same instances in.

### `CreateMediatorOptions`

```ts nocheck
interface CreateMediatorOptions {
  behaviors?: readonly PipelineBehavior[];
}
```

### `Mediator`

```ts nocheck
class Mediator implements MediatorPort {
  register(ctor, handler, options?: RegisterOptions): void;
  use(behavior: PipelineBehavior, options?: RegisterOptions): void;
  send<TResponse>(request: Request<TResponse>, ctx?: RequestContext): Promise<TResponse>;
  registeredRequestTypes(): readonly string[];
}
```

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `register(ctor, handler, options?)` | Registers the one handler for a request class, keyed by the class name. A second registration for the same name throws `HandlerAlreadyRegisteredError` unless `options.allowReplace` is true. |
| `use(behavior, options?)` | Appends a behavior to the pipeline (the first added is outermost). Each behavior class may be used once; a second throws `BehaviorAlreadyRegisteredError` unless `allowReplace` is true, in which case the new instance takes the old one's place in the order. |
| `send(request, ctx?)` | Runs the request through every behavior to its handler and returns the handler's result. Throws `HandlerNotRegisteredError` if no handler is registered. A handler's error reaches the caller unchanged. |
| `registeredRequestTypes()` | The names of every request class with a handler, sorted, as a new array each call. |

### `RegisterOptions`

```ts nocheck
interface RegisterOptions {
  allowReplace?: boolean;
}
```

`allowReplace: true` lets a registration replace an existing one of the same name. It exists for
development servers that re-run registration code on hot reload. Leave it off in production.

### `MediatorPort`

```ts nocheck
interface MediatorPort {
  register(ctor, handler, options?: RegisterOptions): void;
  registeredRequestTypes(): readonly string[];
  send<TResponse>(request: Request<TResponse>, ctx?: RequestContext): Promise<TResponse>;
}
```

The three methods a library needs from a host app's mediator. Depend on this type (not on the
`Mediator` class) in code that should work with any mediator of the same shape. `Mediator` implements
it.

### `HandlerNotRegisteredError`

Thrown by `send` when no handler is registered for the request's class name. `requestName` holds the
name.

### `HandlerAlreadyRegisteredError`

Thrown by `register` on a duplicate class name. `requestName` holds the name.

### `BehaviorAlreadyRegisteredError`

Thrown by `use` when a behavior of the same class is already installed. `behaviorName` holds the name.

## The pipeline

### `PipelineBehavior`

```ts nocheck
interface PipelineBehavior {
  invoke<TRequest extends Request<TResponse>, TResponse>(
    request: TRequest,
    next: Next<TResponse>,
    ctx?: RequestContext
  ): Promise<TResponse>;
}
```

A step that wraps every request. Call `next()` to continue; return or throw without calling it to stop
the request before the handler.

### `Next`

```ts nocheck
type Next<TResponse> = () => Promise<TResponse>;
```

The rest of the pipeline, as seen from inside a behavior.

## Locking

### `MutexBehavior`

```ts nocheck
class MutexBehavior implements PipelineBehavior
```

Takes the keys a request declares with `mutexKey()` for the length of the request. All keys are taken
together or none; a held key throws `MutexHeldError` at once; keys are released on every exit. Locks
are held in memory, per instance, per process. No constructor arguments.

### `HasMutexKey`

```ts nocheck
interface HasMutexKey {
  mutexKey(): string | readonly string[];
}
```

Implemented by a request that needs a lock. Return one key or several.

### `isMutexed`

```ts nocheck
function isMutexed(req: unknown): req is HasMutexKey
```

True when the value has a `mutexKey` method.

### `MutexHeldError`

Thrown when a key is already held. `key` holds the key.

## Auditing

### `AuditBehavior`

```ts nocheck
class AuditBehavior<TInfo extends AuditInfo = AuditInfo> implements PipelineBehavior {
  constructor(options: AuditBehaviorOptions<TInfo>);
}
```

Writes one `AuditEntry` for each request that implements `HasAuditInfo`: outcome `'ok'` when the
handler returns, `'fail'` when it throws (the error is then rethrown unchanged). `auditInfo()` is read
after the handler has run. A request whose `details.columnsPatched` is an empty array is not recorded.

### `AuditBehaviorOptions`

| Option | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `appendEntry` | `AuditWriter<TInfo>` | Required. Stores one row. Receives `(entry, info)`. |
| `mapError` | `AuditErrorMapper` | Required. Turns a thrown error into `{ code }` for the row. |
| `appendLogEntry` | `AuditLogWriter<TInfo>` | Optional. Also copies each row into a general log as a `LogEntry`. Needs `logSource`. |
| `logSource` | `string` | The `source` value for mirrored log entries. |
| `redactSecrets` | `SecretsRedactor` | Replaces the default redaction of `details`. |
| `defaultActor` | `string` | The actor recorded when `send` had no context. Default `'system'`. |
| `reportFailure` | `AuditFailureReporter` | Called when a writer throws. Default `console.error`. |

### `AuditWriter`

```ts nocheck
type AuditWriter<TInfo extends AuditInfo = AuditInfo> = (entry: AuditEntry, info: TInfo) => Promise<void>;
```

### `AuditLogWriter`

```ts nocheck
type AuditLogWriter<TInfo extends AuditInfo = AuditInfo> = (entry: LogEntry, info: TInfo) => Promise<void>;
```

### `AuditErrorMapper`

```ts nocheck
type AuditErrorMapper = (error: unknown) => { code: string };
```

### `SecretsRedactor`

```ts nocheck
type SecretsRedactor = (input: Record<string, unknown>) => Record<string, unknown>;
```

### `AuditFailureReporter`

```ts nocheck
type AuditFailureReporter = (message: string, context: Record<string, unknown>) => void;
```

### `AuditInfo`

```ts nocheck
interface AuditInfo {
  action: string;
  resourceId?: string;
  details: Record<string, unknown>;
}
```

What a request reports about itself. Extend it to add your own fields and read them in your writer.

### `HasAuditInfo`

```ts nocheck
interface HasAuditInfo<TInfo extends AuditInfo = AuditInfo> {
  auditInfo(): TInfo;
}
```

### `isAuditable`

```ts nocheck
function isAuditable(req: unknown): req is HasAuditInfo
```

True when the value has an `auditInfo` method.

### `AuditEntry`

```ts nocheck
interface AuditEntry {
  schemaVersion: 2;
  id: string;
  timestamp: string;
  actor: string;
  action: string;
  outcome: AuditOutcome;
  details: Record<string, unknown>;
  error?: { code: string; message: string };
  correlationId?: string;
  commandName?: string;
  durationMs?: number;
  resourceId?: string;
}
```

The row `AuditBehavior` builds and hands to your writer.

### `AuditOutcome`

```ts nocheck
type AuditOutcome = 'ok' | 'fail' | 'denied';
```

`AuditBehavior` writes `'ok'` and `'fail'`. `'denied'` is there for rows your own code writes, for
example from a permission behavior.

### `auditEntryToLogEntry`

```ts nocheck
function auditEntryToLogEntry(entry: AuditEntry, source: string): LogEntry
```

Converts an audit row to the general log shape: level `info` for `ok`, `warn` otherwise; event type
`audit`; the audit id and resource id added to `details`.

### `redactSecrets`

```ts nocheck
function redactSecrets(input: Record<string, unknown>): Record<string, unknown>
```

Returns a copy in which every value under a secret-looking key is `[REDACTED]`. A key looks secret when
it contains `token`, `secret`, `password`, `api_key` (or `apikey`, `api-key`), `authorization`,
`cookie`, `jwt`, `bearer`, `private_key` or `signature`, in any letter case. It looks inside nested
objects and arrays to four levels.

## Logging

### `LoggingBehavior`

```ts nocheck
class LoggingBehavior implements PipelineBehavior {
  constructor(sink?: MediatorLogSink);
}
```

One line per request: `[mediator] Name ok (1.2ms)`, or `[mediator] Name FAIL (0.4ms):` with the error,
which is then rethrown. Writes to `console.log` unless you pass a sink.

### `MediatorLogSink`

```ts nocheck
type MediatorLogSink = (line: string, error?: unknown) => void;
```

### `LogEntry`

```ts nocheck
interface LogEntry {
  schemaVersion: 1;
  timestamp: string;
  level: LogLevel;
  source: string;
  eventType: LogEventType;
  event: string;
  component?: string;
  message?: string;
  actor?: string;
  userId?: string;
  requestId?: string;
  correlationId?: string;
  durationMs?: number;
  outcome?: LogOutcome;
  error?: LogErrorDetails;
  details?: Record<string, unknown>;
  raw?: string;
}
```

A general-purpose log record that an audit row can be mirrored into. Nothing in the library writes one
unless you pass `appendLogEntry`.

### `LogLevel`

`'debug' | 'info' | 'warn' | 'error' | 'fatal'`. The same values as a runtime array: `LOG_LEVELS`.

### `LOG_LEVELS`

`['debug', 'info', 'warn', 'error', 'fatal']`, read-only.

### `LogEventType`

`'audit' | 'error' | 'request' | 'system' | 'agent'`. The same values as a runtime array:
`LOG_EVENT_TYPES`.

### `LOG_EVENT_TYPES`

`['audit', 'error', 'request', 'system', 'agent']`, read-only.

### `LogOutcome`

`'ok' | 'fail' | 'denied' | 'unknown'`.

### `LogErrorDetails`

```ts nocheck
interface LogErrorDetails {
  name?: string;
  message: string;
  code?: string;
  stack?: string;
}
```

## HTTP: `@garkpit/mediator/http`

### `ok`

```ts nocheck
function ok<T>(data: T, init?: OkInit): Response
```

A JSON response `{"ok":true,"data":…}`. Status 200 unless `init.status` says otherwise.

### `OkInit`

```ts nocheck
interface OkInit {
  headers?: Record<string, string>;
  status?: number;
}
```

### `fail`

```ts nocheck
function fail<Code extends string = string>(
  error: ApiErrorShape<Code>,
  init?: { statusOverride?: number; table?: Record<string, number> }
): Response
```

A JSON response `{"ok":false,"error":{…}}`. The status is `init.statusOverride` if given, otherwise
the code looked up in `init.table`, otherwise in `DEFAULT_STATUS_FOR_CODE`.

### `ApiErrorShape`

```ts nocheck
interface ApiErrorShape<Code extends string = string> {
  code: Code;
  message: string;
  details?: unknown;
}
```

### `DEFAULT_STATUS_FOR_CODE`

| Code | Status |
|---|---|
| `VALIDATION_FAILED` | 400 |
| `UNAUTHORIZED` | 401 |
| `NOT_FOUND` | 404 |
| `CONFLICT` | 409 |
| `MUTEX_HELD` | 409 |
| `PRECONDITION_FAILED` | 412 |
| `INTERNAL` | 500 |
| `UPSTREAM_FAILED` | 502 |

### `statusForCode`

```ts nocheck
function statusForCode(code: string, table?: Record<string, number>): number
```

The status for a code from the table given (default `DEFAULT_STATUS_FOR_CODE`). Unknown codes give 500.

### `readBoundedBody`

```ts nocheck
function readBoundedBody(request: Request, limit: number): Promise<Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>>
```

Reads a Fetch API request body into memory, up to `limit` bytes. A declared `content-length` over the
limit is refused before reading; a longer stream is cancelled as it passes the limit. A request with no
body gives an empty array. Throws `RequestBodyLimitError`. (Here `Request` is the Fetch API's, not the
mediator's.)

### `RequestBodyLimitError`

Thrown by `readBoundedBody`. `limit` is the limit in bytes; `declared` is the `content-length` the
client sent when that is what was over, otherwise `null`.

## Single-file entry points

Each source file is also importable on its own, for code that wants one piece without the rest (the
objects are the same ones the main entry exports):

`@garkpit/mediator/Request`, `/Handler`, `/Mediator`, `/RequestContext`, `/PipelineBehavior`,
`/HasMutexKey`, `/HasAuditInfo`, `/MutexHeldError`, `/audit-types`, `/log-types`, `/redactSecrets`,
`/behaviors/MutexBehavior`, `/behaviors/AuditBehavior`, `/behaviors/LoggingBehavior`, `/http`.

`@garkpit/mediator/Request` has no imports at all, which makes it the right entry for request classes
shared with browser code.
